fieldsRead.text: Radboud’s Communication Science studies how media inform, influence and entertain people. It combines communication theory, psychology and social context with quantitative, qualitative and experimental research, a compulsory internship and a bachelor thesis.

The UCR programmes offer related study of media, persuasion, human behaviour and empirical inquiry. One develops marketing and organisational applications; the other combines communication with digital systems and cognition. They do not reproduce Radboud’s complete communication-science methods sequence, compulsory internship or bachelor thesis. Technical AI study is not a substitute for specialist human-machine communication research.

A communication-focused programme combining media and film analysis, rhetoric and persuasion, social psychology and empirical methods, with marketing and organisational applications. It offers substantial related study of messages, mediated culture and influence, but does not reproduce Radboud’s full specialist methods sequence, compulsory internship or bachelor thesis.

A programme connecting media, persuasion and cultural interpretation with AI systems, data analysis and human cognition. Programming, machine learning and AI planning explain how digital systems work; they complement communication study rather than replace specialist research on human-machine interaction.

selectedDescriptions.name: Personal & Professional Development

content.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
content.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
content.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
content.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Mandatory first-year academic writing, research literacy, reflection and civic development.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. selectedDescriptions.name: Marketing & Consumer Engagement

content.description2: This course unpacks what drives consumer engagement with brands and how marketers build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key marketing concepts, consumer psychology, AI/technology-driven marketing innovation, and brand and communication strategies. Students will explore real-life case studies, develop a strategic marketing plan and learn how marketers build sustainable brand strategies.
content.profile: Connects marketing strategy and consumer psychology to responsible brand development and customer engagement. Students study strategic planning, customer experience, qualitative and quantitative insights, brand identity, digital marketing and behavioural framing. Applied projects analyze a company's strategy and response to disruption, design a brand, and investigate a consumer phenomenon using academic literature and primary and secondary evidence. Customer-journey mapping translates findings into recommendations.
content.topics: Strategic marketing planning; Marketing mix; Customer centricity and experience; Consumer journeys; Market research and augmented insights; Brand identity and image; Brand partnerships; Digital and social marketing; Responsible marketing; Consumer psychology; Nudging and framing; Emerging technologies and marketing agility
content.methods: Marketing-strategy case analysis; Advertising-campaign analysis; Kapferer brand-identity prism; Brand design; Primary and secondary consumer research; Consumer-journey mapping; Disruption-response planning

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Studies persuasive marketing messages and consumer engagement as a specific media-influence application.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Marketing & Consumer Engagement examines consumer psychology, marketing strategy, responsible brand development and customer engagement. Students analyse a company strategy, design a brand and investigate a consumer phenomenon using academic literature and primary and secondary evidence. Digital marketing and customer-journey mapping connect analysis with practical recommendations.

selectedDescriptions.name: Market Research

content.description2: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas. Ready to turn curiosity into career skills? Perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Plans and carries out applied market research into customer opinions and business decisions; a complementary empirical application, not a dedicated communication-effects project.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas—perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.

selectedDescriptions.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations

content.description2: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
content.profile: Introduces entrepreneurship and core business functions through the development of a startup concept. Students use design thinking to discover customer needs, define a problem, generate and prototype solutions, and construct value propositions and business models. Marketing, finance, operations, human resources and funding inform a coherent business plan and investor pitch. Entrepreneurial cases and a startup simulation examine decision-making, early growth and business lifecycles, with attention to societal impact and sustainability.
content.topics: Entrepreneurial mindset and pathways; Business environments, ownership and competition; Customer needs; Value propositions; Business models; Marketing and sales; Finance and accounting; Venture funding; Operations and human resources; Competitive positioning; Startup growth and business lifecycles; Sustainability and societal impact
content.methods: Design thinking; Customer-needs discovery; Ideation and prototyping; Value Proposition Canvas; Business Model Canvas; Business planning; SWOT and risk assessment; Startup simulation

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Introduces the business setting for consumer communication and enables the subsequent applied market-research course.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.

selectedDescriptions.name: Research Methods & Statistics

content.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
content.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
content.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
content.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Introduces research design and statistics for empirical communication questions.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Research Methods & Statistics introduces research design, operationalisation, measurement, sampling, surveys and experiments. Students study descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression using R and R Commander. A group project develops a research plan and instruments, collects and analyses data, and reports findings under research-ethics and privacy requirements.

selectedDescriptions.name: Leadership Communication

content.description2: This course blends theory with practice from both fiction and the real world, helping you develop essential leadership skills. Learn how to inspire teams, sharpen your communication, take ethical decisions, and lead with confidence.
content.profile: Studies leadership communication through leadership theory, persuasion and practical rhetorical work. Students compare contemporary leadership approaches and examine emotional intelligence, gender, culture and ethics. Literary characters, film and speeches provide material for analyzing effective and ineffective leadership. Students interview a real leader, analyze the leader's communication challenge in an advisory report, and develop a public address presenting their own ethical leadership vision.
content.topics: Leadership models and approaches; Transformational, authentic and adaptive leadership; Servant leadership and followership; Emotional intelligence; Leadership ethics; Gender and culture in leadership; Persuasion and organizational communication; Leadership in literature and film; Storytelling and public speaking; Personal leadership vision
content.methods: Leadership-theory application; Literary and film-based leadership analysis; Professional interviewing and note collection; Leadership-discourse analysis; Communication-advisory report development; Rhetorical speechwriting and storytelling

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Studies organisational communication and how leaders address and influence others.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: This course blends theory with practice from both fiction and the real world, helping you develop essential leadership skills. Learn how to inspire teams, sharpen your communication, take ethical decisions, and lead with confidence.

selectedDescriptions.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership

content.description2: This course offers Liberal Arts and Sciences students a deep dive into the psychological, social, and structural dynamics that shape workplaces. Through interactive case discussions, simulations, and real-world insights, students develop critical skills in motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and culture. By synthesizing research and applying theory to practice, participants gain the tools to navigate and influence diverse organizational environments effectively.
content.profile: Examines organizational behaviour at individual, group and organizational levels. Topics connect personality, perception, emotions and motivation to teams, leadership, power, conflict, structure, culture and change. Students design research plans for organizational cases and conduct a brief systematic literature review using PRISMA reporting tools. Workshops develop literature searching, study selection, source appraisal and synthesis, linking organizational-psychology evidence to practical questions and recommendations.
content.topics: Diversity, equity and inclusion; Job attitudes and satisfaction; Emotions, stress and workplace health; Personality and individual differences; Perception and decision-making; Motivation; Group behaviour and work teams; Human resource systems; Communication, conflict and negotiation; Leadership, power and politics; Organizational structure; Organizational culture and change
content.methods: Organizational case analysis; Research design and hypothesis formulation; Systematic literature review; PRISMA flow diagrams and checklists; Database searching and study screening; Source-quality appraisal and evidence synthesis

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Studies psychological and group dynamics through which organisational messages operate.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership examines the psychological, social and structural dynamics of organisations. Case discussions and research-based frameworks address motivation, leadership, group dynamics, organisational culture, power, conflict and change.

selectedDescriptions.name: AI Ethics

content.description2: Explores philosophical foundations and implications of AI. Examines the history of AI, ethical issues like interpretability, bias and alignment, debates about AI consciousness and implications for human nature.
content.profile: Examines AI through ethical theory and psychological accounts of human behaviour and interaction. Ethical debates address fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Psychological perspectives consider development, clinical care, social and organizational relationships, forensic applications and cognitive neuroscience. Students synthesize literature and apply ethical frameworks in an analytical psychology project and a research-grounded podcast, with a creative communication component.
content.topics: Algorithmic fairness and bias; Privacy and surveillance; Responsibility and accountability; Human-value alignment; Moral status of AI; Existential risk and democratic implications; Trust and agency in human-AI interaction; AI in clinical care; Child development and AI; Social and organizational effects of AI; AI in forensic psychology; Cognitive and socioemotional development; AI consciousness and sentience
content.methods: Ethical-framework application; Philosophical argument evaluation; Psychological-literature synthesis; Theory-based analysis of AI applications; Research podcast scripting, recording and editing

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Examines ethical questions raised by AI-mediated communication.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness, privacy, responsibility, human-value alignment, moral status and political or existential risks. Students apply ethical frameworks to questions about human behaviour and interaction, synthesise research in an analytical psychology project, and produce a research-based podcast.

selectedDescriptions.name: Decision-making in AI

content.description2: Introduces planning techniques for AI systems in deterministic and non‑deterministic environments. Addresses uncertainty, partial observability, resource planning and optimizing behaviour under constraints.
content.profile: Develops the mathematical foundations of intelligent-agent decisions under uncertainty. Probability and Bayesian networks support belief updating and inference, while temporal models address changing environments. Decision theory, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems connect uncertainty to policies and expected utility. Multi-agent decisions introduce strategic and collective interaction, and probabilistic programming provides a framework for expressing models. Students work through equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.
content.topics: Conditional probability, independence and Bayes' rule; Bayesian networks; Temporal probabilistic models; Hidden Markov models and dynamic Bayesian networks; Expected utility; Markov and partially observable decision processes; Exploration-exploitation trade-offs and bandits; Competitive and cooperative multi-agent interaction; Negotiation, auctions and voting; Probabilistic programming
content.methods: Probabilistic inference; Bayesian-network modelling; Temporal probabilistic modelling; Expected-utility analysis; Sequential decision modelling; Game-theoretic analysis; Probabilistic programming

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Studies AI planning under uncertainty, partial observability and resource constraints; a technical foundation for autonomous systems, not research on human responses to conversational agents.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Decision-making in AI examines how intelligent agents make decisions under uncertainty. Students study probability, Bayesian networks, temporal models, expected utility, Markov decision processes, partial observability and bandit problems. Multi-agent decisions and probabilistic programming extend the analysis, supported by equations, numerical examples and scientific papers.

selectedDescriptions.name: Optimization Methods in AI

content.description2: Covers computational methods for search problems in complex and adversarial environments. Includes uninformed and informed search, local and global search, adversarial games and constraint satisfaction problems.
content.profile: Studies search and optimization for rational agents in known, complex and adversarial environments. Students move from uninformed and heuristic search to local and global optimization, first- and second-order methods and population approaches. Adversarial search, constraint satisfaction, linear programming and discrete optimization extend the toolkit. Laboratories and projects require algorithm tracing, implementation and evaluation and experimental investigation of small intelligent systems.
content.topics: Intelligent and rational agents; Uninformed and informed search; Heuristic functions; Search in complex environments; Local and global optimization; First- and second-order optimization; Population methods; Adversarial games; Constraint satisfaction; Linear programming; Discrete optimization
content.methods: Uninformed and heuristic search; Local and global search; First- and second-order optimization; Population-based optimization; Adversarial search; Monte Carlo tree search; Constraint-satisfaction algorithms; Linear programming; Discrete optimization; Algorithm implementation and experimental evaluation

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Studies search, games and constraint optimisation by rational AI agents; a complementary technical explanation of autonomous-system decisions rather than human-machine communication itself.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Optimization Methods in AI studies search and optimisation for rational agents. Topics include uninformed and heuristic search, local and global optimisation, adversarial search, constraint satisfaction, linear programming and discrete optimisation. Laboratory exercises and projects develop algorithm implementation, evaluation and experimental investigation of small intelligent systems.

selectedDescriptions.name: Introduction to Data Science

content.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
content.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
content.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
content.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Introduces descriptive analysis and visualisation of evidence used to study media and audiences.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.

selectedDescriptions.name: Machine Learning

content.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
content.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
content.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
content.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Develops classification and predictive models for analysing digitally generated information.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Machine Learning introduces methods for understanding data and making predictions, including linear regression, classification, resampling, shrinkage, tree-based methods, support vector machines and clustering. Real-world examples illustrate the methods, their strengths and limitations.

selectedDescriptions.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision

content.description2: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
content.profile: Examines how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognize structures and objects. Spatial and spectral representations, colour and image statistics support filtering, segmentation, curve and feature detection, tracking and object classification. Students use Python and OpenCV to implement image-processing techniques, investigate spectral representations, and build a recognition pipeline whose performance is benchmarked on previously unseen images.
content.topics: Spatial and spectral image representations; Cameras and calibration; Colour models and quantization; Image histograms; Point operators; Linear and nonlinear filters; Edges and contours; Mathematical morphology; Image segmentation; Curve and corner detection; Feature detection and tracking; Object localization and classification; Recognition performance
content.methods: Python and OpenCV programming; Image filtering; Histogram and point transformations; Morphological image processing; Hough transform; Image segmentation; Feature matching and tracking; Recognition-pipeline design; Benchmark evaluation on unseen images

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Analyses visual data processing relevant to image-based digital media and machine interpretation.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Image Processing & Computer Vision studies how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognise structures and objects. Topics include colour, image statistics, filtering, segmentation, feature detection, tracking and object classification. Practical work uses Python and OpenCV to develop and benchmark an image-recognition pipeline on previously unseen images.

selectedDescriptions.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning

content.description2: Explores theory and practice of neural networks. Students build basic networks and progress to complex networks for computer vision, and discuss recent developments in large language and image generation models.
content.profile: Develops neural-network theory and practical implementation in Python, Keras and TensorFlow. Students build and train simple networks before studying multilayer architectures, backpropagation, regularization and model evaluation. Later work applies deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects construct predictors for tabular data and investigate an independently chosen image- or text-based prediction problem, with experimental results reported in a paper.
content.topics: Perceptrons and ADALINE; Multilayer neural networks; Gradient descent and backpropagation; Bias-variance trade-off and regularization; Computation graphs; Network architectures and interpretation; Computer vision; Time-series learning; Text classification and generation; Transformers and large language models; Feature engineering; Predictive performance
content.methods: Python programming; Keras and TensorFlow network implementation; Gradient-descent training; Backpropagation implementation; Neural-network performance evaluation; Tabular prediction; Image classification; Text classification and generation; Deep-learning experimental design

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Actual neural networks, text classification/generation, transformers and empirical model evaluation support investigation of AI-mediated content; not specialist human-machine interaction research.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Neural Networks & Deep Learning combines theory with practical Python, Keras and TensorFlow implementations. Students build and train networks, study backpropagation, regularisation and model evaluation, and apply deep learning to computer vision, time series and text, including transformers. Projects investigate prediction problems and report experimental results.

selectedDescriptions.name: Introduction to Programming

content.description2: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.
content.profile: Introduces computational problem-solving and programming in Python. Students develop structured programs using branching, iteration, functions and data collections, then progress to recursion, exception handling and object-oriented programming with inheritance. Elements of logic, sets and enumeration support computational reasoning. Exercises and projects require students to write, trace, test, debug and explain programs that solve problems of moderate complexity.
content.topics: Python language fundamentals; Strings and input/output; Branching and loops; Functions; Tuples, lists, sets and dictionaries; Aliasing and cloning; Recursion; Exceptions and assertions; Object-oriented programming; Inheritance; Computational problem-solving
content.methods: Structured programming in Python; Object-oriented programming; Recursive problem-solving; Program tracing; Testing and debugging; Exception handling

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Develops programming skills for analysing and constructing digital communication systems.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Introduces programming and computer science. Covers structured programming, data constructs, testing, debugging and object‑oriented programming with Python, and develops computational problem‑solving skills.

selectedDescriptions.name: Mathematical Methods

content.description2: Introduces linear algebra (vectors, matrices, eigenvalues) and calculus (limits, differentiation, integration) to construct and solve equations. Provides problem‑solving skills applicable across disciplines.
content.profile: Develops single-variable calculus and related mathematical tools for modelling scientific problems. Functions, limits and differentiation lead to optimization, Taylor series, complex numbers, integration and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica, including numerical approximation. A project implements, analyzes and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and explanation of the computational results.
content.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models
content.methods: Analytical differentiation and integration; Taylor approximation; Newton's method; Numerical integration; Euler's method; Analytical solution of differential equations; Computer algebra with Mathematica; Dynamic-model implementation and analysis

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Provides mathematical foundations for modelling AI systems used in human-machine communication.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Mathematical Methods develops foundational techniques in differentiation, integration, complex numbers and differential equations. Students solve problems analytically and with Mathematica. A project implements, analyses and adapts a dynamic model, requiring interpretation of its behaviour and computational results.

selectedDescriptions.name: Philosophy of Mind

content.description2: Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.
content.profile: Examines minds, selves and conscious experience through historical and contemporary philosophy. Personal identity and self-knowledge are considered alongside Buddhist accounts and neuropsychological cases. Behaviourism, physicalism, functionalism and their critics frame the mind-body problem. Later inquiries address machine consciousness, virtual worlds, dreaming, perception, transformative experience and the value of experience. Essays develop independent philosophical interpretations and arguments.
content.topics: Persons and personal identity; Psychological and narrative theories of identity; Buddhist non-self; Split-brain cases and self-knowledge; Behaviourism; Physicalism and functionalism; Mind-body problem; Content externalism and internalism; AI intelligence and consciousness; Virtual reality; Dreaming and perception; Transformative experience; Value of conscious experience; Animal minds
content.methods: Close philosophical reading; Conceptual analysis; Reconstruction and evaluation of arguments; Comparison of theories of mind; Literature-based philosophical research

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Investigates mind and consciousness in relation to artificial agents and human experience.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.

selectedDescriptions.name: Qualitative Research Methodology

content.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
content.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
content.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
content.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Teaches qualitative interviewing and interpretive research on social experience.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.

selectedDescriptions.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

content.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
content.profile: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
content.topics: Civil society; Social trust and social capital; Hegemony; Critical theory; Public spheres, digital publics and counterpublics; Solidarity and civil repair; Civil sphere; Social movements and intersectionality; Migrant solidarity; Civil society under authoritarianism; Decolonial critique; Public sociology
content.methods: Comparative social-theory analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Document and secondary-source analysis; Structured reflection on civil-society engagement or observation; Sociological research design

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Examines social capital, solidarity and civil society as settings of collective communication.

selectedDescriptions.name: Psycholinguistics

content.description2: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Examines psychological and neural language processing in human communication.

content.profile: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.

selectedDescriptions.name: Social Psychology

content.description2: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
content.profile: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
content.topics: Social cognition and person perception; The self and self-motives; Social influence; Persuasion, attitudes and behaviour; Group processes; Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination; Prejudice reduction; Interpersonal aggression; Prosocial behaviour; Interpersonal attraction and close relationships
content.methods: Critical appraisal of empirical social-psychology research; Literature synthesis; Theory-guided hypothesis formulation; Research design for a proposed social-psychology study

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Examines social influence and group behaviour relevant to persuasive media effects.

selectedDescriptions.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods

content.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
content.profile: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
content.topics: Experimental, nonexperimental and quasi-experimental designs; Statistical inference; Correlation and regression; Model assumptions and diagnostics; Group comparisons; Covariate adjustment; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed designs; Categorical outcomes; Latent constructs and scale reliability; Effect size and power; Statistical reporting
content.methods: R and R Commander data analysis; Multiple linear regression and dummy coding; Regression diagnostics; t-tests and nonparametric alternatives; ANOVA and ANCOVA; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed-design ANOVA; Logistic regression; Exploratory factor analysis; Principal component analysis; Cronbach's alpha; APA statistical reporting

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Actual experimental/nonexperimental/quasi-experimental designs, regression, ANOVA/ANCOVA, categorical/latent models and R reporting support behavioural communication research; no required communication dataset assumed.

selectedDescriptions.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication

content.description2: Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
content.profile: Teaches rhetorical analysis and persuasive communication through classical history, theory and practice. Students study Greek and Roman rhetoric, the five canons, types of discourse, persuasive appeals, argumentation and fallacies. Written exercises, debates and public speeches develop invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery. An applied project creates narrative and storytelling material for an immersive educational setting concerned with Zeeland's climate and community.
content.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication
content.methods: Rhetorical text analysis; Stasis analysis; Argument invention and arrangement; Stylistic analysis and composition; Structured debate; Persuasive speechwriting and delivery; Educational storytelling design

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Examines rhetorical appeals and public persuasion, a direct contribution to communication influence.
selectedDescriptions.selectedDescription: The Art of Rhetorical Communication develops rhetorical analysis, academic writing and oral presentation. Students examine classical Western roots and the canons of rhetoric, and learn to construct, organise and support persuasive arguments. Historical and contemporary examples connect rhetorical theory with practical communication.

selectedDescriptions.name: Style & Meaning

content.description2: Explores how linguistic choices inform meaning and interpretation in literary and non-fiction contexts. Introduces theoretical frameworks for close reading and addresses power dynamics, obligation, uncertainty and ideological undertones in language.
content.profile: Studies how linguistic choices produce meaning and interpretive effects, principally in literary texts but also in nonfiction. Students connect linguistic description to interpretation across grammar, discourse and cognition. Stylistic frameworks address foregrounding, dialogue, narration, modality, transitivity, deixis, schemas, construal and text worlds. Frequent analysis exercises lead to an original, research-supported stylistic analysis of a selected text.
content.topics: Foregrounding and deviation; Morphology, syntax and lexical semantics; Register and cohesion; Dialogue and turn-taking; Cooperative principle; Speech and thought presentation; Modality and point of view; Transitivity and ideology; Narrative urgency; Figure and ground; Deixis and deictic shift; Schemas, scripts and prototypes; Cognitive grammar and construal; Text-world theory; Negation and lacuna
content.methods: Linguistic stylistic analysis; Close textual analysis; Discourse and conversation analysis; Speech and thought presentation analysis; Modality and transitivity analysis; Deictic and cognitive-grammar analysis; Text-world analysis; Framework-based interpretation supported by retrievable textual evidence

selectedDescriptions.contribution: Develops close linguistic/stylistic analysis, primarily using literary texts, with some non-fiction application; contributes a particular form of message analysis rather than general media-effects research.

selectedDescriptions.name: Persuasive Communication

content.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
content.profile: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.
content.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication
content.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle

selectedDescriptions.name: Creative Communication Laboratory

content.description2: Explores meaning-making through creative expression. Students study and practice poetic forms, experiment with sonic poetry, performance and other unconventional forms of communication, engage with theoretical texts and produce their own creative work.

Students move from lyric foundations to constrained and experimental forms, attending to sound, rhythm, imagery, voice and embodiment. Close reading and creative workshops lead into an independent traditional or hybrid project grounded in scholarship and aesthetic traditions. Revision and reflection require students to justify formal, conceptual and procedural choices.

content.methods: Close poetic reading and listening; Constraint-based composition; Poetic and performative experimentation; Structured drafting and revision; Critical analysis of creative decisions; Independent practice-based creative inquiry

selectedDescriptions.name: Media & Race

content.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
content.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.

selectedDescriptions.name: The Documentary

content.description2: Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.
